questions.question: How did the study of antibiotic resistance illustrate the principles of evolution?
questions.solution_html:
• The study of antibiotic resistance illustrates the principle of evolution by showing
  • how bacteria adapt to survive when exposed to antibiotics. When antibiotics are used,
  • bacteria with random genetic mutations that make them resistant can survive and
  • reproduce, while others die. Over time, the population shifts to mostly resistant
  • bacteria, demonstrating natural selection—only the fittest survive and pass on their
  • genes. This real-time evolution is a clear example of how selective pressure (like
  • antibiotic use) leads to changes in populations, just as Charles Darwin described in his
  • theory of evolution. (U, CO6)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: theory of evolution. (U, CO6)

questions.question: Discuss on visualisation and live imaging in disease diagnosis and therapeutics.
questions.solution_html:
• Visualization and live imaging in disease diagnosis and therapeutics involve advanced
  • techniques that enable real-time or detailed visualization of cells, tissues, and organs
  • to understand disease progression and guide treatment.
  • • Advanced visualization technologies transform imaging data into intuitive 3D or 4D
  • images allowing precise identification of disease sites and detailed anatomical
  • understanding.(Techniques include CT scans, MRI, and advanced software that
  • enhance clarity to distinguish tumors, tissue damage, or abnormalities, aiding quicker
  • and more accurate diagnosis)
  • • Live imaging captures dynamic biological processes in real-time, such as cell
  • movement, blood flow, or drug interactions, using methods like fluoroscopy,
  • ultrasound, real-time MRI, and fluorescence microscopy. This enables monitoring of
  • therapeutic interventions' effects at cellular or tissue levels, optimizing treatments and
  • understanding drug mechanisms. ( A, CO5,CO7)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: understanding drug mechanisms. ( A, CO5,CO7)

questions.question: What is speciation, and what are the mechanisms that can lead to it?
questions.solution_html:
• Speciation is the process by which new species are formed from existing ones. It
  • happens when populations become reproductively isolated and can no longer
  • interbreed.Mechanisms leading to speciation include geographic isolation (allopatric
  • speciation), reproductive isolation within the same area (sympatric speciation), and
  • variations like peripatric and parapatric speciation. (U, CO6)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: variations like peripatric and parapatric speciation. (U, CO6)

questions.question: Briefly explain the concept of independent assortment.
questions.solution_html:
• Independent assortment is the principle that genes for different traits separate
  • independently of each other during the formation of gametes in meiosis. This means
  • the inheritance of one gene does not affect the inheritance of another, leading to
  • genetic variation. (U,CO4)

questions.final_answer: genetic variation. (U,CO4)

questions.question: What is one limitation of Whittaker’s five-kingdom classification system?
questions.solution_html:
• One limitation of Whittaker’s five kingdom classification is that it places very diverse
  • organisms together in the same kingdom. For example, unicellular algae are classified
  • in the Protista kingdom, while multicellular algae are placed in the Plantae kingdom,
  • even though they share similarities. This leads to inconsistency in grouping related
  • organisms.(An, CO6)

questions.question: What is the function of the nucleus in eukaryotic cells?
questions.solution_html:
• The nucleus in eukaryotic cells functions as the control center, storing the cell’s
  • genetic material (DNA) and regulating activities like growth, protein synthesis, and
  • cell division. It also protects DNA, oversees DNA replication and transcription, and
  • produces ribosomes in the nucleolus.(U,CO1)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: produces ribosomes in the nucleolus.(U,CO1)

questions.question: Define the term 'genetic code.'
questions.solution_html:
• The genetic code is the set of rules by which the sequence of nucleotides in DNA or
  • RNA is translated into the sequence of amino acids in a protein. Each group of three
  • nucleotides, called a codon, codes for a specific amino acid or a stop signal during
  • protein synthesis.( K,CO1)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: protein synthesis.( K,CO1)

questions.question: What is the role of spindle fibers during cell division?
questions.solution_html:
• The role of spindle fibers during cell division is to attach to chromosomes and help
  • separate the sister chromatids or homologous chromosomes, pulling them towards
  • opposite poles of the cell. This ensures that each daughter cell receives an equal and
  • accurate set of chromosomes. (U,CO2)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: accurate set of chromosomes. (U,CO2)

questions.question: What is the significance of biodiversity hotspots?
questions.solution_html:
• Biodiversity hotspots are regions with a high variety of endemic species that exist
  • nowhere else and have lost a significant portion of their natural habitat. Their
  • significance lies in being critical areas for conservation because they support rich
  • biodiversity, provide essential ecosystem services like climate regulation, pollination,
  • and water purification, and help maintain ecological balance. Protecting these
  • hotspots also safeguards the livelihoods of people who depend on these
  • ecosystems.(U,CO3)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: ecosystems.(U,CO3)

questions.question: Expand NMR and mention its principle. Type Questions
questions.solution_html:
• NMR stands for Nuclear Magnetic Resonance. Its principle is based on the fact that
  • certain atomic nuclei have a magnetic property called spin. When placed in a strong
  • magnetic field, these nuclei absorb and re-emit radiofrequency energy at a
  • characteristic frequency. This resonance gives detailed information about the
  • molecular structure and environment of the atoms in a sample.(K,CO3)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: molecular structure and environment of the atoms in a sample.(K,CO3)

questions.question: Give an account on the challenges and applications of biotechnology and nanotechnology in the modern world
questions.solution_html:
• Biotechnology is used for medical therapies, genetically modified crops, waste
  • treatment, and environmental conservation. Challenges include high costs, regulatory
  • hurdles, ethical issues, and potential risks like biosecurity concerns.
  • Nanotechnology offers advancements in medicine, electronics, and environmental
  • cleanup by manipulating materials at the nanoscale. Its challenges involve safety and
  • toxicity risks, scaling up production, regulatory gaps, ethical concerns, and
  • interdisciplinary collaboration.
  • Both fields hold great promise but require cautious management to balance benefits
  • and risks.(A,CO6)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: and risks.(A,CO6)

questions.question: Explain the concept of the central dogma of molecular biology.
questions.solution_html:
• The central dogma of molecular biology explains that genetic information flows from
  • DNA to RNA and then to proteins. DNA is first transcribed into RNA, which then
  • serves as a template for synthesizing proteins through translation. This process is
  • essential for gene expression and controlling cellular functions.(U,CO1)
questions.source_exam: First Semester MGU-UGP/MGU-BBA/MGU-BCA Honours Examinations November 2025
questions.final_answer: essential for gene expression and controlling cellular functions.(U,CO1)

questions.question: Explain the concept of independent assortment and how it contributes to genetic diversity.
questions.solution_html:
• Independent assortment is the principle that genes for different traits separate
  • independently during the formation of gametes in meiosis. This means the inheritance
  • of one gene does not affect the inheritance of another. It increases genetic diversity by
  • creating new combinations of alleles, contributing to variation among
  • offspring.(U,CO4)
